title: Six Breathing
passages:
Quill read it the way she did everything, at the speed of a woman writing it down while she talked.

"Berth book, low gate, the Kettle. Entry. Eleven seconds off the master slate of the salvage boat Marrow, read into this book on the boat's own request." Paper moved. "The voice is the tech's. Logged as hers."

"Read it," Sol said. Her hand was flat on Dey's chest, not pressing, just resting there like she was holding down a hatch.

The channel gave them a woman clearing her throat. Twice. It was not a pleasant noise. It was Wren's throat, fourteen months ago, working around something it did not want to say.

"Throat logged," Quill said. "Then: *help is already coming.*" She put the lift on it without meaning to, up on the last word. "There's a lift on the end of *coming*. Up and not down. I'm told to log the lift. It's logged."

"Lift logged," Nia said, on her knees with the paper log open and a pencil stub in her fist.

"The last line I have off this boat isn't slate, it's paper. Hour, then: *Dey Okafor, not breathing.* Entered by N. Vos." The pencil-scratch of Quill's stylus came over the speaker, small and awful. "Both parts are true and they don't sit together, and I'm obliged to write them one under the other. So I have."

Wren stood under the beam with the spent gray spool wound twice around two fingers. She had said the same eleven seconds herself, flat and dry, with Salas close enough to hear her teeth. Hearing them come back in a stranger's mouth was worse, and she couldn't have said why.

"Come alongside," Sol said. "I'll stand at your counter and say all of it again with my face on it. Then you look at me and write what you see."

"The book takes what the channel carried," Quill said. "It came over the channel. If I put your face in place of it, I've shaded it, and I don't shade. Come stand in front of me if it helps you. It'll cost you four of your forty and change the entry not at all."

Sol said a word the channel did not need. Quill logged that too, because she logs everything.

Under Sol's hand Dey's heel was going against the deck mat, fast, in threes. Nobody had a use for that yet.

"One more entry I'm obliged to make before that count runs out." A page turned somewhere above the waterline. "The bell column."

Bayo Adisa was at the rail with his cuffs up, the orange splice-knots on them gone dark with wet. He did not turn around. Ivo Salas sat on the winch drum with his forearms on his knees, watching the water the way a man watches a door he already knows is locked.

"I'll take it from anyone aboard the Marrow," Quill said. "I can't take it off the water. I can't take it secondhand. And I won't leave it blank, because a blank goes into that column as a blank, and a blank is worth the same to the next man who reads it as a lie would be."

East of them the barge sat dark where it had been leaning all night, riding the chop without a light on it, close enough now that Wren could hear its hull slap.

Sol's hand went up and down on Dey's chest for both of them.

"Who had the bell tonight," Quill said. It went out over the open channel and across the whole low gate, into every boat tied up there, every slate with the channel open. "On the record. Who had the bell."

Nobody on the aft deck moved except the man who couldn't breathe.

"Bayo Adisa." He said it into the channel, which meant he said it from the low gate to the east mole and into every slate with the channel open. Then his shoulders came down an inch, like a man setting down a case he'd carried up too many stairs. "I had the bell."

"Your mark," Quill said.

He drew it in the air with his thumb, three strokes and a bar across them. "Three-notch-over-bar. Every pilot on this coast signs the bell column with his own, so no man can stand at a rail in the morning and say *not me, that was somebody else's watch.* Mine's three-notch-over-bar. It's on fourteen months of pages and it's on one report."

"Say the rest in order," Quill said. "The book likes order."

He didn't sit down. "Fourteen months ago I had a diver on my line at forty-two meters in the salvage tower. My wire was running over the lip of the pocket door and it was chafing. Weather was coming up the coast and there was a barge at my shoulder that wanted the site and would pay well for a pilot who could hold the Stair." He turned his cuffs over, the knots on them dark and stiff with salt. "I put my hand on the lever and cut the line. One pull. Clean, no jerk on him. He'd have felt it go slack and thought I was taking up the slack."

"And the report," Quill said.

"I wrote Ivo Salas lost at forty-two meters. I signed it. The mark's on it and it's mine."

Ivo Salas got up off the winch drum. It took him a while and nobody moved to help. "Put the other name in with it," he said. "Not *the diver*. I've been carrying a hole where your face ought to be since the day I went down, and I want the two things in one mouth."

"On the record. Bayo Adisa cut the ascent line of Ivo Salas at forty-two meters, and Bayo Adisa wrote Ivo Salas off as lost." The stylus went, small and dry over the speaker. "Both names logged together. They'll sit together in this book from now until the paper goes. I don't shade, so if one of you turns out sorry, it'll be written down right beside the other one."

"He isn't," Salas said.

"I'm not," Bayo said.

"Logged," said Quill.

Salas looked at him a long moment, the way a man looks at a tool he's about to have to use. "Fourteen months I've had nothing there. Turns out a face wasn't what I needed. A voice does it. Now I know exactly whose voice to listen for on a wire."

"Bell column," Quill said. "Low gate, the Kettle, this count. Bell-mark three-notch-over-bar struck." Paper moved. "Bayo Adisa is off the bell."

Nobody up the steps said anything, and that was the whole low gate hearing it.

"Berth nine-oh-two," Quill went on, because she says the true price when it costs the most. "Bell-tender's berth, above the waterline, at the Kettle. Struck in this count, forfeit in this count. It's gone as of now and it doesn't come back and I'm obliged to say the number out loud so you know what you spent."

Bayo's fingers were working at nothing, tying a knot in air and pulling it tight and starting another. "You could have waited for the count to run out."

"You'd have known by morning. Then I'd have shaded a day for you, and you'd have known that too, and you'd have had to carry both."

Under Sol's hand Dey's heel had stopped going in threes. It started again.

East of them the dark hull slapped the chop, close now, close enough that Wren could hear water going in and out of a scupper. Then a lamp came on it. Not a signal lamp, not swung or hooded at anyone's face — a work lamp unhooked and set low, the kind you use for counting.

It lit a wet deck, five crates lashed under a net, and one more crate standing apart and streaming, and a boot planted beside that crate, and above the boot a knee, and above the knee a man who did not shade his eyes.

Rusk came over the rail with the sixth crate under his arm and set it on the deck mat between Sol's knees and Dey's chest, then planted his boot on the corner. Water ran off the sole in a thin stream. "I'm Anselm Rusk," he said. "Collector for the Factor. The Factor doesn't take a short count. You owe him one crate, and you're one short."

Sol didn't move her hand from Dey's chest. Dey wasn't breathing under it. The lung rig was still east on Quill's power barge, committed until the bell hit ten, and they had minutes left on the clock.

"The Marrow," Rusk said. "Hull, drum, and bell. That's my price for the crate. The Factor wants a boat, not medicine he can't sell. And my berth rides on this debt, so I'm not leaving here empty-handed."

Wren said, "You can't take a boat with no one to run it. Sol's missing hours she won't count, Dey's not breathing, and Nia's never taken the helm through the Stair with a dead diver on the mat."

Rusk smiled. It didn't reach his eyes. "Then you should have thought of that before you chose children over a cold-case payoff. I can see you deciding, Sol. I can see you weighing whether the crate's worth the boat. You don't have to say anything yet. I'll wait while you finish bluffing."

The dark barge hummed at the rail, its engine ticking as it cooled. A line from its bow reached out, slack in the chop, waiting for a hand to make it fast to the Marrow's empty mooring bitt.

"The bell's counting," Salas said from the winch drum. "When it hits zero, the channel shuts. You're not towing anything out through the Stair after that."

"I know," Rusk said. "That's why I'm here now."

He shifted his weight on the crate. The wood creaked. Under Sol's hand, Dey's chest stayed still.

Sol looked up. Her eyes were flat, the way they got when she couldn't remember a name but refused to ask for it. "You want the Marrow? You'll have to take her with Dey still on board. And I'm not signing her over."

"Good," Rusk said. "I don't want your signature. I want the boat. And I'll wait right here until you decide that keeping it costs more than it's worth."

The lamp on his barge swung once, casting his shadow long across the deck mat, across the crate, across Sol's hand on Dey's chest.

Sol took her hand off Dey's chest and the deck heard it, the small tacky sound of skin leaving skin.

"Quill. Open channel, and write the hour first." She wiped her palm on her thigh and stood up. "Sol Ferreira, master of the Marrow. I'm putting a number in your book and I want it said plain, not spelled soft."

"Say it," Quill said.

"Fourteen months on that tower. Eight hours and forty minutes I can't find." Sol said it the way she said a depth. "I keep the running count in pencil inside my locker lid, because my own head won't hold it. The last one was an hour and six, up at your counter, deciding between two children and twelve thousand. I only know the length because the tech read it back to me off my own wire."

"Logged," Quill said. "Eight hours, forty minutes."

"I can't hold a boat past a bell." Sol turned so the work lamp on the dark barge got her face. "If I take this hull out through the Stair in the dark with a hole in my night, I'll hand whoever's at the wheel the wrong order and never know I gave it. Ask me what happened when the crates broke loose in the chop. Go on."

Rusk shifted his boot on the crate. "I'd love to."

"I was on the drum," Sol said. "Then I was here. Salas's leg was cut free and my hands were on the rail. That's the whole of it. Ask the girl. She writes it down."

"Twelve-nineteen," Nia said, not looking up. "Crates broke at twelve-sixteen. Vos took the helm. Salas cut the port lashing with the rigging knife at twelve-nineteen. Ferreira gave no order."

"Nineteen minutes," Sol said. "Gone out of the middle of a channel."

Wren said, "Sol—"

"Not now." Sol picked up the paper log off Nia's knee, turned it around, and held it out to the girl with the pencil stub laid on top. "Deck's yours, Nia Vos. Say it back."

Nia's hands were filthy and steady. "Deck's mine."

"Say the hour and write it."

"Twelve-twenty-two. Vos has the deck of the Marrow, given by Ferreira." The pencil scratched. She wrote *given*, not *lost*, and nobody corrected her.

"Touching," Rusk said. "The clock's at four minutes, captain. Children and paper."

"Then take the offer, it's cheaper than waiting." Sol faced the rail, the channel speaker, the whole low gate stacked up its steps in the dark. "Book. Sol Ferreira offers her own name in the column where Dey Okafor's is. My bond, my labor, against the six berths. He's fifteen, he's got a chest full of the deep, and I've got years in. Write mine and strike his."

The stylus did not move. When Quill came back she was small and even, the way she got when the price was going to land on somebody.

"I can't. Not shading — can't. A diver's bond is his hands and his hours, and I can hold both of them to a berth. You've just told the low gate on an open channel that you can't be held to an hour of your own head." A breath. "A captain's bond with no hull under it isn't worth six berths, it's worth a page. If I wrote your name there I'd be writing a value I know is false with my mark under it, and the next man to read that book would be reading a lie and calling it the Kettle's word. I don't shade. Your name isn't money tonight."

Rusk laughed. It came out of him warm and surprised, and he took his boot off the crate to do it.

"There. There it is." He spread his hands. "I had you down for a bluff. Everybody's got a number, I said, she picked children over a payoff so her number must be somewhere south of twelve thousand and she's just walking me toward it." He shook his head, almost fond. "Your number's nothing. You just priced yourself at zero in front of every slate in the low gate."

"It's still above yours," Sol said. "Yours is a boot."

"Four minutes is three now." He drew his knife, a short rigging knife with a hooked point for wet line, and did not point it at anybody. He crouched and laid the edge against the Marrow's mooring line where it ran up out of the chop to the low gate ring. "Nobody's signed me anything. So I've no claim yet. But a hull with no line on it, no hand on the tiller, adrift inside the gate at slack water, is derelict. Derelict's the Factor's, and then it's mine, and I'll have taken it honest." The hook slid under the strands. "Say the word, captain. Say *take the boat* and I'll sheath this."

Behind him Bayo's fingers were tying a knot in nothing, pulling it tight, starting the next one.

"Say it," Rusk said. "Say *take the boat*, and I'll sheath this."

"Deck," Wren said. "I want the drum."

Nia's pencil came off the paper. "Why."

"Because there's one pull left in it, and one pull is worth something to a man who's about to be a skipper." Wren put her palm flat on the drum housing. The battery box under it was still warm from forty-two meters. "One pull is rated for one diver on one wire. In the Stair that's enough to walk a hull's head around the second turn before the ebb sets you up on the tram roof. That's the whole of what I'm selling. It's not much."

"It's a tow with my own boat," Rusk said.

"It's a tow with somebody who knows the marks." Wren turned to the channel speaker. "Book. Two entries, and I'm not the one who can't shade, so hear them off me."

"Ask," Quill said.

"His berth first. Number, and when it goes."

"Entry." Paper moved. "Anselm Rusk, collector for the Factor, master of the barge *Tally*, berth four-one-four. Forfeit at slack water, because he came up one crate short and the Factor doesn't take a short count." A breath. "That's the true price and it lands on you tonight, Rusk, not on me."

"And second," Wren said.

"No other pilot on this coast will lift a hand for him," Quill said. "That isn't shading either, it's arithmetic. Bayo Adisa was the last man who knew the Stair, and I struck him off in this count with all of you listening, and I can't unstrike him."

"A boat called *Tally*," Wren said. "Naturally."

Rusk stood in his own work light with the knife still under the mooring line and did his sums out loud, because he liked the sound of them. "A hull's worth more than a page."

"A hull aground on a tram roof at slack water is worth a swim," Wren said.

Bayo hauled the barge's bow line in out of the chop, took two turns and a hitch around the Marrow's stern bitt, and stepped over the rail onto the *Tally*'s wet deck. He put both hands on the wheel. Then he said the rest into the channel, flat, with no lift on the end of any of it.

"Line's fast. Drum takes the strain, not your bitts. Marks for tonight: Bell One at the low gate ring, tram roof on the second turn, and keep her off it. Pilot on the water, Bayo Adisa, three-notch-over-bar, struck off the bell this count."

Every slate in the low gate heard the mark and the strike in one mouthful.

Wren knew the shape of that kind of promise. She had heard him build one before, warm and easy, out of nothing at all. She said nothing. She had spent her whole working life handing people the soft version of things, and she had just stopped.

Rusk sheathed the knife slowly, so the steps could watch him choose it. "The line stays on your ring. Slack water's twenty minutes out and after that she's mine and I don't want her. Put it in the book and I'll take your crate's worth of wire."

"Entry." The stylus went. "One pull of the Marrow's drum, traded to Anselm Rusk for the sixth medicine crate, delivered into the count. Mooring line to remain fast to the low gate ring, by his word on the open channel." Paper moved again. "The derelict claim is a claim and I've written it as one, under his name, and it doesn't stand while that line's fast. Rusk, you heard me. It's written where you can't take it back."

"I heard you," Rusk said.

"Salas, the crate goes up the steps," Nia said. "Ferreira stays where she is."

Sol didn't argue. Salas got the crate up onto his hip, and Nia said the hour out loud, and nobody wrote it down.

The stylus went while he was still climbing. "Six of six crates received. Six berths, above the waterline, the Kettle. Indenture, one: Okafor, Dey. The count stands at six and it stands at one and I've put both in."

The bell went over the water. Two minutes, or one.

Sol's hand was back on Dey's chest, and under it the boy stopped moving.

Not the threes. Not the small hitch he had been giving her all night. Nothing at all, and her palm kept going up and down with her own breathing.

"Entry, and I'll make it before anything else happens on that deck," Quill said, "because you'll want it in order. The lung lavage rig did not go east. It has been under my tarp at the low gate since the bell struck ten."

Under Sol's palm, nothing moved.

"Say it again," Wren said.

"I don't repeat to soften it. Under my tarp, out of the rain, since ten."

"You told us it was committed to the power barge at the east mole."

"It was committed to the power barge. That's written and it's true and I'll read it back to you if you want the wording. The commitment ended when the bell struck ten and the barge came back to the steps and I took the rig off it myself." Paper moved, small and dry over the speaker. "You asked me when it came free. Nobody asked me where it sat. I answer the question I'm asked. That isn't shading. That's the book."

Wren laughed, one note, nothing behind it. "We ran the Stair on that. I went down to forty-two on that."

"Since ten," Quill said. "Do your own arithmetic, I'm not reading it into the book."

"I ran a cold-box by hand for a year rather than ask one person for one thing," Nia said, pencil already going. "So I know the shape of it. You wanted him to have a mark first."

"A bond wants a mark and not a mouth," Quill said. "I can put a rig on a bonded man. I can't put it on a name with an empty line under it, and his line is empty, and I don't shade a line to make my night easier."

"Well," Rusk said, from the crate he was no longer standing on. "There's a lesson in that for anyone who trusts a woman with a book."

"There's a lesson in that for anyone who trusts a man with a knife," Sol said.

"Both logged," said Quill. "Vos has the deck. What's the order?"

"Bring the rig in," Nia said. "Wren, hands off my drum. Salas, get back down here."

The power barge came in under the low gate steps with its deck lights burning for the first time all night, and the light came across the water and up the Marrow's side and lay down on the aft deck, and everybody on it had to look at what they'd been listening to. Dey's face was the color of wet ash. Bayo's cuffs were stiff with salt. Six crates stood in a row with the net folded back off them, and the Marrow's own mooring line ran up out of the light to the ring, fast, the way Rusk's word had left it.

Salas came down the steps with empty hands and knelt and got the boy's head up onto his knee without being asked.

The rig came over the rail in two pieces: a pump head on a battery pack, and a warmed tank with a hose coiled on top. Quill's people ran a cable back to the power barge and the gauge on the tank went green. "Blood heat," the one with the cracked goggles said. "Ninety-eight and no more. Hotter and you cook the lining out of him and then he's got nothing to breathe with."

"And the canister?"

"Sintered mesh. The deep plates out on it gray, you'll see." She held up two cartridges in her fist, one in each hand, like a woman showing a card player her whole hand. "Two. Four minutes a pass. After that he's on his own lungs and his own luck."

They put the gobbet in Dey's mouth and the pump started and the warm water went down into him, and Wren sat on the deck with the hose in both hands and the gray spool still wound twice around her fingers, and the first pass came back out into the tray pearly and slow, and then not pearly.

Nia counted out loud, because everything on this boat got said out loud now. "One."

Nobody spoke for four minutes.

"Two. Three. Four." The boy's chest went up on its own under Sol's hand and Sol took her hand away and left it in the air above him, not touching. "Five. Six."

"Thirteen-oh-four," Nia said, and wrote it. "*Okafor, Dey. Six breaths, own.*"

Dey's eyes came open on the work light and went around the deck and stopped on Bayo Adisa standing at the rail between the two hulls with his hands on it.

"Does anyone aboard wish to enter thanks to the pilot," Quill said. "On the record. Tonight."

The pump ran. The channel slapped the hulls. Nobody said a word.

"No thanks entered," Quill said.

"Log it plain," Bayo said. "That's the true price too."

"Logged."

Out on the *Tally*, Bayo's hand went to the key and turned it, and the engine turned over once, caught nothing, and stopped, and the dark barge swung a half meter on the bow line and sat there in the light with water going in and out of its scupper.

Wren looked at the drum's battery gauge. One bar. One pull, already sold, and the channel shutting.

"Book," she said. "Put down that the pilot's boat won't start."
